..
KEY MESSAGE 1...

An upper level disturbance is currently located over the Upper
Great Lakes and it will be lifting across southern Ontario and
into western Quebec for today. At the surface, a cold front is
located well west of the area over the Ohio Valley and Midwest.
Surface warm front will be lifting across the area this morning
and a surface trough ahead of the main front will be approaching
the area for this afternoon into this evening. This will be the
focus for showers and thunderstorms, which look to develop by
the early to mid afternoon hours.

There looks to be sufficient shear and instability for organized
storms today. The 00z HRRR and 00z SPC HREF both shows
instability should reach the 1000-2000 J/kg range, especially
for southern areas. 0-6 km bulk shear should be around 30 kts
today. As a result, storms look to organize into small bows or
lines by late this afternoon into this evening, bringing a
threat for straight-line wind damage. Some the stronger storms
could contain some hail as well. An isolated tornado is possible
for any supercells ahead of the main line and the 00z HRRR does
suggest there may be enough low-level helicity, although Sig Tor
parameters looks to max out around 1-2 today, mainly for 
eastern areas. AI/ML guidance continues to show the potential 
for damaging winds and an isolated tornado across the region for
today as well and has been showing this signal for the past few
days. SPC has expanded the Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5) and it 
now is in place for nearly the entire ALY Forecast area. 

Storms may linger into the evening, but will start to diminish
by midnight, as the best forcing shifts eastward and the loss
of daytime heating allows instability to wane.   

KEY MESSAGE 2...

In addition to the severe threat, there will be the potential
for heavy rainfall and localized flooding this afternoon into
this evening. PWAT values will be surging to 1.50 to 2.00 inches
for this afternoon and evening thanks to the low-level southerly
flow in place. Dewpoints will be reaching well into the 60s to
near 70 by late this afternoon, so there will be plenty of
moisture available. Rainfall rates can easily reach 1-2 inches
per hour in this type of environment.

CAMs suggests that several rounds of storms are possible and
some areas may see training of precipitation. Some of the CAMs 
(especially the RRFS) suggests that localized rainfall totals 
may exceed 4 inches. While the placement has varied somewhat
from run-to-run, the consensus in ensembles seems to suggest
that southern areas (Ulster and Dutchess Counties) may have the
highest potential for heavy rainfall, as cellular activity may
occur in addition to a main line of storms. As a result, have
issued a Flood Watch for the potential for flash flooding for
Ulster and Dutchess Counties, which also matches up with the
Slight Risk (Level 2 of 4) for Excessive Rainfall from WPC.
Urban and low lying areas would be the most susceptible to
flooding, which may result in damaged and impassable roadways.
As always, travelers are reminder to need cross flooded
roadways.

In addition to southern areas, other parts of the area may 
still see flooding rainfall and some guidance does suggest parts
of the Lake George Region and southern VT could see repeated 
downpours as well, so will need to monitor trends and possibly 
expand the current Watch further north.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

The storm's main cold front will be crossing on Friday. A few
additional showers or thunderstorms are possible on Friday,
mainly for southern and eastern areas, but coverage will be
lower than Thursday. There won't be as much instability and
shear, so storms won't be able to become severe and probably
won't be widespread enough to cause any additional flooding.
The threat for additional precipitation will end from west to
east during the afternoon hours with the passage of the cold
front.

Over the weekend, high pressure will allow for dry weather and
seasonable conditions. Plenty of sunshine is expected on
Saturday with highs in valley areas in the upper 70s to low 80s.
Dewpoints will be more comfortable compared to recent days, with
values in the 50s to low 60s. It will turn slightly more humid
and warmer on Sunday, but it looks to stay dry with a partly
sunny sky and highs reaching the lower to middle 80s.
